title: Blended & Flipped Learning

pts: Blended learning deliberately combines classroom and online or self-study components, each doing what it does best.
This differs from simply adding optional digital extras onto an otherwise unchanged course.
This connects directly to Unit 18's principle that technology should serve the aim, applied at course-design scale.

items: Read two short course descriptions.
For each component of each course, ask: what is it for, and why is it here rather than in class?
Decide which course is a designed blend and which simply adds digital extras.
Take one of your own units and list any outside-class components it already has.
Justify each in one sentence, or redesign it.
In a teacher circle, each teacher presents one component and the group asks, ‘Why outside?’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Course A: normal lessons from the coursebook. The school has also bought an app; learners can use it if they wish.

Course B: each week, learners listen to a five-minute audio explanation and complete a short vocabulary sheet at home. In class, they use that language in a pair task, and the teacher gives feedback on the task.

blocks.x: Course A has digital extras; Course B is a blend, in which each part has a job and depends on the others. This applies Unit 18’s principle, that technology serves the aim, at course level.

body: Purpose: to contrast design with addition. Content: left, a plain building with a satellite dish awkwardly bolted to its side, labelled ‘add-on’; right, a building whose rooms are connected by a staircase, some rooms marked ‘class’ and others ‘home’, labelled ‘blend’. Style: architectural, clean. Board version: two rectangles, one with an attachment and one divided into connected rooms.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared course-component table.

blocks.x: A two-column table in the planning notebook: ‘component’ and ‘why here?’.

pts: In a flipped model, input (a lecture, an explanation, a reading) happens outside class; class time is reserved for interactive application.
This protects scarce class time for exactly the interaction and negotiation of meaning central to this tier (Unit 30).
It requires reliable learner engagement with the outside-class input — a real design and motivation challenge.

v: 5–8 minutes at home; one full lesson in class
A short recorded explanation or a printed explanation sheet; a pair task

items: Choose one grammar point or text that you would normally explain in class.
Record a short explanation (under six minutes) on your phone, or prepare a one-page illustrated sheet.
Share it two days before the lesson, with two simple questions to answer.
In class, check the questions quickly, then move straight into a communicative task using the language.
Circulate, notice problems and give feedback.
Flip a reading text instead: learners read at home, and class time goes to discussion and a follow-up task.
Support: the explanation also available in the home language.
Challenge: learners prepare three example sentences of their own before class.

lines: Outside class: a four-minute voice recording by the teacher: When I was a child, I used to walk to school with my cousins… with two questions: What did the teacher use to do? What does used to show?
In class: a ‘Then and now’ pair interview about childhood in the learners’ town or village, followed by a short group report.
T: Tell your partner three things you used to do when you were small, and ask three questions.
A: I used to climb the mango tree behind my grandmother’s house.

blocks.x: The flip protects class time for exactly the interaction and negotiation of meaning described in Unit 30.

body: Purpose: to show the reversal of input and practice. Content: top row, ‘traditional’: a teacher talking in class, then a learner struggling alone at home; bottom row, ‘flipped’: a learner listening to a phone at home, then learners talking in pairs while the teacher circulates. Style: simple, side-by-side panels. Board version: two rows of two boxes with arrows.

items: WhatsApp (free) voice notes to share short explanations with families.
YouTube (free) with unlisted videos for teacher-made explanations.

blocks.x: A one-page illustrated explanation sheet sent home in the notebook.

pts: Explicit grammar explanation, vocabulary pre-teaching, and extensive input (Units 31–32) transfer well to outside-class time.
This frees class time from content delivery that doesn't inherently require a group or a teacher present.
This connects to Unit 19's homework-design principles, applied specifically within a flipped structure.

v: A unit plan; a list of its activities

items: List every activity in one unit.
Mark each activity: I (needs interaction or the teacher) or O (can be done alone).
Check the O activities: explicit grammar explanation, vocabulary pre-teaching, extensive reading and listening, controlled practice.
Choose one or two O activities to move outside class.
Design each as a short, clearly bounded homework task (Unit 19).
Learners sort activity cards into ‘home’ and ‘class’.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A sorted list for a unit on festivals:

lines: O: read a graded text about Pongal and Onam; learn ten festival words with a word card set; watch a short explanation of the present simple passive (is celebrated, is made).
I: interview a partner about a family festival; plan a class festival guide in groups; give feedback on each other’s drafts (Unit 43).

blocks.x: Extensive reading and listening (Units 31 and 32) are natural outside-class components: they need time and quantity, not a group.

body: Purpose: to show which activities travel well outside class. Content: two illustrated menu cards. The ‘Home’ menu lists ‘read’, ‘listen’, ‘learn words’, ‘watch an explanation’; the ‘Class’ menu lists ‘talk’, ‘solve’, ‘negotiate’, ‘create together’. Style: playful, café-menu design. Board version: two lists under headings.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for textbook-linked content in English and Indian languages.

blocks.x: Graded readers from the class library and printed word cards.

pts: Task-based work, discussion, negotiation of meaning, and collaborative production belong in class, where interaction is possible.
This protects the interactive core of Tier II's methodology from being crowded out by content delivery.
If class time is still mostly spent on input delivery, the flip likely hasn't actually happened yet.

v: A watch or phone timer; an observation grid

items: In a flipped lesson, a colleague times three kinds of activity: teacher explaining, learners working alone, learners interacting.
Repeat in a normal lesson on similar content.
Compare the proportions.
If teacher explanation still takes most of the flipped lesson, decide what else can move outside.
A learner volunteer keeps the timer and shows the result on the board at the end.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Normal lesson (40 minutes): explaining 22, working alone 12, interacting 6.
Flipped lesson (40 minutes): explaining 6, working alone 8, interacting 26.

blocks.x: If class time is still mostly explanation, the flip has not yet happened.

body: Purpose: to show how a flip reallocates class time. Content: two horizontal bars representing forty-minute lessons, divided into coloured segments for ‘explaining’, ‘alone’ and ‘interacting’; the interacting segment is small in the first bar and large in the second. Style: clean, data-graphic. Board version: two bars divided with chalk lines.

items: A phone stopwatch or timer app (free).

blocks.x: A wall clock and a tally grid on paper.

body: Bergmann and Sams (2012) began recording lessons partly for learners who missed class for sports and other activities. The model grew from a practical problem rather than a theory.

pts: A flipped model only works if learners genuinely engage with the outside-class component before arriving.
Short, low-stakes accountability checks (not full tests) at the start of class support this without undermining motivation.
This connects to Unit 19's feedback-loop principle — engagement needs some acknowledgment to be sustained.

v: 2–5 minutes at the start of class
Three quick questions on the outside-class input

items: As learners settle, display or read three quick questions about the outside-class material.
Learners answer in their notebooks or tell a partner.
Take a show of hands or fingers (one, two or three correct).
If many learners have not engaged, run a three-minute catch-up summary with a learner who did.
Learners bring one ‘question I still have’ from the outside-class material; the teacher answers the most common.
Support: questions with picture or multiple-choice options.
Challenge: learners write a fourth question for the class.

blocks.x: Door-check questions after a flipped explanation of used to:

lines: True or false: we use used to for things that happen now.
Complete: When I was five, I ___ to sleep in the afternoon.
Write one thing you used to do.

blocks.x: Such checks acknowledge outside-class work without turning it into a test; Unit 19 showed that engagement falls when such work is never followed up.

body: Purpose: to show a light accountability check. Content: learners entering a classroom, each holding up one, two or three fingers, while the teacher at the door smiles and ticks a small chart. Style: friendly, brisk. Board version: three hand symbols and a tally.

items: Google Forms (free) as a short pre-class check for learners with access.
Kahoot! (free basic version) for a quick in-class check where a projector is available. [VERIFY current free-tier player limit]

blocks.x: Three questions on the board; fingers raised.

pts: Unit 18's digital-divide concern applies directly here — a flipped model assumes reliable outside-class access.
Offline or low-bandwidth equivalents for outside-class components protect learners without consistent digital access.
Equity should be checked explicitly before adopting a blended model at scale, not discovered as a problem afterward.

items: Survey learners: access to a phone (own or shared), internet, times of access, space to study, and support at home.
Group results into three levels: regular online access, occasional access, no access.
For each outside-class component, design a version for each level.
Check that the in-class task does not depend on having used the online version.
Ask the school to open a room with a few devices before or after school.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Three routes for one outside-class explanation:

lines: Regular access: a four-minute video on YouTube.
Occasional access: the same explanation as a WhatsApp voice note, downloadable when data is available.
No access: a printed sheet with the same examples, or a ten-minute session in the school library before class.

blocks.x: Checking equity before adopting a blended model, rather than discovering exclusion afterwards, applies Unit 18’s concern about the digital divide.

body: Purpose: to show equitable routes to the same lesson. Content: three roads, one marked by a laptop, one by a basic phone, one by a printed page, all leading to the same classroom door. Style: inclusive, clear. Board version: three lines converging on a square.

items: Google Forms (free) for the access survey, with a paper version for learners without devices.

blocks.x: Printed explanation sheets and a library-period catch-up slot.

pts: Map each unit's components explicitly onto outside-class or in-class time, using the criteria from this poster's earlier cards.
This extends Unit 11's unit-sequencing principles into a blended structure, rather than a purely in-class one.
Communicate the structure clearly to learners — a blended model that isn't understood as such quickly falls apart in practice.

v: Teacher activity; A2–B2 learners for step 5
A unit plan (Unit 11); a two-row planning grid

items: Draw a grid with the days or lessons of a unit across the top and two rows: ‘outside class’ and ‘in class’.
Place each activity in its row, using the sorting from point 3.
Check the links: every outside task should prepare for something in class.
Add the door checks (point 5) and the offline routes (point 6).
Share a simplified version of the map with learners at the start of the unit, and explain why it is organized this way.
Display the map on the wall and tick off each stage as the class completes it.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A two-week map for a B1 unit, ‘Our neighbourhood’:

lines: Outside, day 1: listen to a voice-note explanation of there is / there are and quantifiers; read a short text about a market in Mysuru.
In class, day 2: door check; information-gap map task; feedback.
Outside, day 3: interview a family member (in any language); note three points in English. In class, day 4: groups compare interviews and plan a guide.

blocks.x: A blended model that learners do not understand quickly collapses; explaining it is part of the design, extending the sequencing of Unit 11.

body: Purpose: to show a unit as two linked rows. Content: a two-row grid with small icons (headphones, book, speech bubbles, pencil) in alternating cells, connected by curved arrows showing each outside task leading to an in-class task. Style: clean, planner-like. Board version: a two-row table with arrows.

items: Google Classroom (free for schools) to post the map and outside-class materials.

blocks.x: The map copied onto chart paper and displayed in class.

pts: Blended and flipped models inherently demand more learner autonomy than a fully in-class model.
This connects to Unit 19's autonomy-readiness calibration — a class not yet ready for this needs more structured scaffolding first.
Building autonomy deliberately, rather than assuming it, makes a blended model more likely to succeed over time.

items: Before starting a blended model, learners complete a short readiness checklist (see model language).
Look at the results: where do most learners need help?
Teach one self-study skill explicitly each week (for example, how to replay a recording, how to note questions).
Begin with very short, structured outside tasks; lengthen them as habits form.
After a month, repeat the checklist and discuss progress with the class.
‘Study buddy’ pairs remind and help each other.
Support: checklist items with pictures and home-language glosses.
Challenge: learners plan one outside-class task of their own choice each week.

blocks.x: A readiness checklist (written for this book):

lines: I know when and where I can study at home.
I can listen to a recording again if I don’t understand.
I write down questions to ask in class.
I can finish a task without someone reminding me.

blocks.x: Holec (1981) defined autonomy as the ability to take charge of one’s own learning; Benson (2011) stresses that it develops through practice and support. A blended model raises the stakes of Unit 19’s readiness calibration, so scaffolding must be deliberate. Unit 48 returns to autonomy.

body: Purpose: to show autonomy developing with support. Content: three bicycles, the first with training wheels and a teacher’s hand on the seat, the second with training wheels only, the third ridden freely towards ‘independent learning’. Style: warm, encouraging. Board version: three simple bicycle outlines.

items: Google Forms (free) for the readiness checklist.

blocks.x: The checklist printed and glued into notebooks.

body: Flip one lesson this month. Choose a grammar explanation you usually give, record it as a voice note or write it as a one-page sheet, and use the lesson time for a pair task. Time how much of the lesson learners spend talking, and compare it with a normal lesson.

dek: Unit 44 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier II by extending skill-integration principles beyond the physical classroom, using class time for what needs it most.

aims.x: Class time is the scarcest resource in language teaching. This unit shows how blended and flipped designs move some work outside the classroom, so that time together is used for what only a group can do, and how to keep such designs fair where devices and connectivity are unevenly shared.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish a designed blended course from a course with digital extras added;
explain the flipped classroom model and its main risk;
decide which activities belong outside class and which inside;
design short, low-stakes checks that sustain outside-class engagement;
plan offline and low-bandwidth routes so that no learner is excluded;
map one unit of work onto a blended structure and explain it to learners;
build the learner autonomy a blended model depends on.

why: Why this matters. Class time is scarce and best spent on interaction — the thing a classroom does that self-study can't. Blended and flipped design protects that time deliberately.

background.x: Blended learning is usually defined as the deliberate combination of face-to-face and online or self-directed learning, designed so that each component does what it does best (Garrison and Kanuka 2004). In ELT, Sharma and Barrett (2007) warned early on against simply bolting technology onto an unchanged course; the design question is not ‘Which app shall I add?’ but ‘Which parts of learning need the teacher and the group, and which do not?’ Tomlinson and Whittaker’s (2013) case studies make the same point: successful blended courses were planned as a whole, with a rationale for each component.

The flipped classroom is one specific blended design. Bergmann and Sams (2012), two US secondary chemistry teachers, popularized recording explanations for learners to watch at home, freeing class time for problem-solving with the teacher present. Abeysekera and Dawson (2015) suggest flipping may help by letting learners pace new input and by making class time more interactive, while noting that much early evidence was descriptive. For language teaching, the logic is strong: interaction and the negotiation of meaning (Unit 30) require other people, while a grammar explanation or a graded reader does not.

The Indian context adds both opportunity and caution. The NEP 2020 devotes a chapter to online and digital education, while insisting that the digital divide must be addressed and that online methods cannot fully replace in-person learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: chapter 24 [VERIFY chapter number]), and the NCF 2023 treats digital resources as supports for, not substitutes for, classroom interaction (NCERT 2023 [VERIFY wording]). National platforms such as DIKSHA offer free textbook-linked content in many Indian languages, and during the pandemic teachers improvised with WhatsApp voice notes, printed worksheets and neighbourhood learning groups. Warschauer (2003) reminds us that access is not just a matter of owning a device: it includes time, space, skills and support at home. A design that ignores these realities widens the gaps it hopes to close. Home languages help too: an outside-class explanation in Kannada or Telugu, followed by English practice in class, may be the most efficient flip of all for beginners.

items: Engagement record. Track door-check results across a unit to see how many learners engage with outside-class work.
Interaction time. Compare the proportion of class time spent on interaction before and after flipping.
Task performance. Assess the in-class task as usual; it shows whether the outside-class input was taken up.
Learner voice. Ask: ‘Did working at home first help you in class? What made it hard?’
How much of your class time is spent on explanation that learners could receive elsewhere?
Which of your current homework tasks are genuinely linked to what happens in the next lesson?
Which learners in your class would be excluded by an online-only design?
How could home languages make outside-class input more accessible?
What self-study skills do your learners already have, and which would you need to teach?
What would you need to explain to parents about a flipped approach?

NCERT. 2023. National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023. New Delhi: National Council of Educational Research and Training.

perm: Surveys about home access touch on family circumstances; keep them anonymous, collect only what you need, and follow school policy on learner data.

terms.def: A planning tool that surveys learners’ access to devices, internet, time and study space, groups them by level of access, and provides a version of each outside-class task for every group, so no one is excluded.
A combination of face-to-face classroom teaching with online or outside-class learning, planned so that each part supports the other (Garrison and Kanuka 2004).
A planning grid showing a unit’s outside-class and in-class activities side by side, so that the teacher can check that every outside task prepares for something in class.
The gap between those who have access to digital devices, the internet and the skills to use them and those who do not.
A model in which learners meet new input outside class, for example through a short video or reading, so that class time can be used for interaction and practice (Bergmann and Sams 2012).
The proportion of class time learners spend interacting in English. It is one measure of whether a change such as flipping the classroom has freed time for practice.

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.
A short, informal check, such as a quick quiz or show of hands, that carries few or no marks and is used to confirm that learners have engaged with preparatory work and to guide the lesson.
Material that learners read, watch or listen to before or between lessons, as in a flipped classroom, so that class time can be used for practice and interaction.
The extent to which learners have the skills, access, habits and confidence to learn independently, often checked with a short checklist before a blended or flipped model is introduced.
